questions.q: Which problem is the clearest fit for two pointers from opposite ends?
questions.explain: Sorted data plus a question about pairs is the classic signal. The other three depend on counts, not order, and fit the frequency counter.
options: Count how many times each product was sold
In payouts sorted by amount, find two that add up to a refund
Find the first order id that appears only once in an unsorted log
Group usernames that are anagrams

questions.q: In a sorted list, amounts[left] + amounts[right] is bigger than the target. Why is it safe to move right one place left?
questions.explain: Every other partner still in range is at least as large as amounts[left]. So amounts[right] is ruled out for good, and dropping it loses nothing.
options: Because the right end is always wrong
amounts[right]'s smallest possible partner is amounts[left], and even that sum is too big, so no pair using amounts[right] can match
Because the left pointer has already checked it
It is not safe; you must also try moving left

questions.q: What invariant makes the pair-sum walk correct?
questions.explain: It holds at the start (the whole array) and each move keeps it true. When the pointers meet, the range holds no pair, so by the invariant none existed.
options: The sum always decreases
If a matching pair exists, both of its entries are between left and right
left is always smaller than the target
The array stays sorted after each step

questions.q: What goes wrong if pair sum uses while (left <= right)?
questions.explain: A pair needs two different positions. left < right guarantees that and also handles empty and one-element lists without special cases.
options: It misses pairs at the ends
When the pointers meet, it adds an entry to itself, so a single ₦5,000 payout "matches" a ₦10,000 target
It becomes O(n²)
Nothing; both conditions are the same

questions.q: At most how many sums does the two-pointer pair search compute on 10,000 sorted payouts?
questions.explain: Each step moves one pointer one place towards the other, and they start n − 1 places apart. The naive version needs up to n(n − 1) / 2 = 49,995,000.

questions.q: Unsorted payouts arrive and memory is plentiful. Which pair-sum approach is usually the better choice?
questions.explain: Two pointers on unsorted data is simply wrong. Sorting first costs O(n log n). The Map is O(n) time; its only price is memory. Two pointers win when the data is already sorted or memory is tight.
options: Two pointers directly on the unsorted list
The Map of seen amounts: O(n) average time, O(n) space, no sort needed
Every pair
Sort, then two pointers, always

questions.q: What happens if you run the two-pointer pair search on unsorted amounts?
questions.explain: The safety argument for each move relies on sorted order. Without it the function returns wrong answers with no error at all, which is the worst kind of bug.
options: It throws an error
It still works, just more slowly
It can silently miss pairs that exist, because "everything further left is smaller" is no longer true
It always returns the first two items

questions.q: Amounts are sorted with amounts.sort() before the pair search. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Use amounts.sort((a, b) => a - b) for numbers. String order puts "100" before "25".
options: Nothing
Without a comparator, sort compares numbers as strings, so [100, 25, 3] stays in that order and the two-pointer argument breaks
sort removes duplicates
sort sorts in descending order

questions.q: Why does in-place dedupe compare ids[read] only with ids[write - 1], the last kept id?
questions.explain: Sorting groups equal values into runs. On unsorted data you would need a Set of seen ids (O(n) space) instead.
options: Because comparing with all kept ids would be too slow to be correct
The array is sorted, so all copies of an id are next to each other; a repeat can only equal the most recently kept id
Because write - 1 is always 0
To save memory

questions.q: Removing every repeat with splice inside one loop looks like a single pass. Why is it O(n²)?
questions.explain: The hidden loop is inside splice. With every id twice, 100,000 ids cause about 2.5 billion moves; the reader/writer version makes one write per kept id.
options: Because the loop runs twice
Each splice shifts every later element one place left, O(n) per removal, and there can be O(n) removals
Because splice sorts the array
It is O(n)

questions.q: What is the main risk of an in-place algorithm like dedupeSorted(ids)?
questions.explain: In-place saves memory by reusing the input. Make it obvious in the name and documentation, and prefer a copy when memory allows.
options: It uses too much memory
It changes the caller's array; code that still needs the original sees the shortened version
It is slower than copying
It only works on strings

questions.q: In container with most water, the left panel is shorter than the right. Why move left and not right?
questions.explain: Moving the taller side can never help: width shrinks and the level is still capped by the short side. Moving the shorter side is the only move that might find a taller, better tank.
options: Because left pointers always move first
Every other tank using the short left panel is narrower and still capped at its height, so none can beat the current one; the left panel is finished
Because moving right would skip the answer only on even lengths
Either works equally well

questions.q: Container with most water uses two pointers although the heights are not sorted. What replaces sortedness in the argument?
questions.explain: Two pointers need a proof that each move is safe, not necessarily sorted data. Sortedness is just the most common source of such a proof.
options: Nothing; the answer is only approximately right
The observation that the shorter side caps the level, which proves each move discards a side that cannot be in a better answer
The heights are sorted internally first
A hash map of heights

questions.q: Which pairing of problem and pointer shape is right?
questions.explain: Pair sum uses opposite ends; the middle of a list uses fast and slow; merging uses one pointer per list, each advancing when its head is taken.
options: Middle of a linked list: opposite ends
Pair sum in a sorted array: fast and slow
Remove duplicates in place: a reader and a writer moving the same way
Merge two sorted lists: fast and slow on one list

questions.q: Why use fast and slow pointers to find the middle of a linked list rather than computing Math.floor(n / 2)?
questions.explain: When the fast pointer (two steps at a time) reaches the end, the slow one (one step) has walked half as far. Both are O(n); fast/slow saves the second walk.
options: Because division is slow
A linked list has no index and no stored length: you would have to walk it once to count and again to reach the middle; fast/slow does it in one walk
Because it gives a different middle
Because arrays cannot be split

questions.q: To find the stop 3 from the end of a linked route in one walk, the lead pointer gets a head start. Of how many stops, and why does it work?
questions.explain: A fixed gap between two same-speed pointers turns "k from the end" into "k behind the lead". If the head start runs out of stops, the route has fewer than k stops.
options: 1 stop, because the trailing pointer moves twice as fast
3 stops; then both move one stop at a time, stay 3 apart, and when the lead falls off the end the trailing pointer is 3 from the end
Half the route, like the middle search
It cannot be done without knowing the length first

questions.q: Why does the middle loop test fast !== null && fast.next !== null?
questions.explain: The order matters too: && stops at the first false test, so fast.next is never read when fast is null.
options: To skip the first node
The fast pointer jumps two nodes; both must exist, or fast.next.next would read a property of null and throw
To make the loop run twice as fast
Because null is a valid stop

questions.q: In Floyd's cycle detection, why must the fast pointer eventually land on the slow one if there is a loop?
questions.explain: Once both are in the loop, the distance from fast to slow (going forward) decreases by 1 per move. A gap that shrinks by exactly 1 must reach 0, within one lap.
options: Because they start at the same place
Inside the loop the fast pointer gains exactly one step on the slow one per move, so the gap shrinks by one each time and cannot jump over zero
Because the loop has even length
It might never meet it; you need a timeout

questions.q: When would you pick a Set of visited accounts over Floyd's method for a forwarding loop?
questions.explain: Both find the loop in O(n) time. Floyd's needs O(1) space. For a modest number of accounts, the simpler code is usually the better engineering choice.
options: When memory is extremely tight
When clarity matters more than memory: the Set version is easier to read and also O(n) time, at the cost of O(n) space
Never; the Set cannot detect loops
When the loop is very long

questions.q: An account forwards money to itself. What does Floyd's method do?
questions.explain: After one move, slow and fast are both at the account again, so they meet; the second phase then starts both at the same account and returns it immediately.
options: Loops forever
Returns null
Detects a loop of length 1 and reports that account as the loop's start
Throws an error

questions.q: Where does the two-pointer walk show up inside databases?
questions.explain: Merge joins, external merge sorts and reconciliations of two sorted files all walk two sorted inputs once each, just like merging two sorted arrays.
options: In the password hashing
In a merge join: both inputs sorted on the join key, one pointer per side, advance whichever key is smaller
In COUNT(*)
Nowhere; databases only use hash tables

questions.q: A developer's two-pointer loop has a branch where neither pointer moves. What happens?
questions.explain: Termination comes from the pointers getting closer on every step. Every branch must move at least one pointer.
options: The branch is skipped next time automatically
If that branch is ever taken, the loop sees the same state again and never ends
The loop becomes O(n²)
Nothing; JavaScript advances loop variables for you

questions.q: A random test only checks that refundPair returns non-null exactly when the brute force finds a pair. Which bug would it miss?
questions.explain: "Found or not" agrees, yet the positions are useless. The lesson's test also checks that each returned pair has i < j and really adds up to the target.
options: Returning null when a pair exists
Returning a pair when none exists
Returning the wrong positions, such as [0, 0], whenever some pair exists
An infinite loop

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 2 + 11 = 13 is too big, so right moves to 7; 2 + 7 = 9 matches at [0, 3]. (4 + 5 would also match, but the walk reaches 2 + 7 first.) A single 5 cannot pair with itself; two separate 5s can.
options: [ 0, 3 ] null null

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1 + 9 = 10 is too small (L), 3 + 9 = 12 is too small (L), 4 + 9 = 13 matches with left = 2, right = 4.
options: found 0 4
LLfound 2 4
LRfound 1 3
RLfound 2 3

questions.q: This dedupe forgets to truncate the array. What does it print?
questions.explain: Only the first write slots hold the answer; the tail keeps whatever was there before. That is why the lesson ends with ids.length = write, or returns write so the caller knows how much is valid.

questions.q: A developer removes adjacent duplicates with splice inside a for loop. What does it print?
questions.explain: After the splice at i = 1, the next 7 slides into position 1, but the loop moves on to i = 2 and never compares it. Changing a list while walking it skips elements (see Why doesn't this work?), and it is O(n²) as well. The reader/writer version has neither problem.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The default sort compares strings: "100" < "25" < "3". Two pointers on that "sorted" list would give wrong answers. Always pass a numeric comparator.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The list is A to F (built backwards). Slow visits B, C, D while fast visits C, E, then null past F. With an even count this loop stops at the second of the two middles, D.
options: C
D
E
A

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: From x the path is x → a → b → c → a …, so the loop starts at a. From b, b is already inside the loop, so the loop "starts" where the walk entered it: at b.
options: x b
a b
a a
null b

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Panels 1 (height 8) and 8 (height 7) are 7 apart: 7 × 7 = 49. The walk checks exactly n − 1 = 8 pairs; the brute force would check 36.

questions.q: What does this print?
What does this print?
questions.explain: On the tie at 400, <= takes from the statement first, so equal entries keep "statement before ledger": the merge is stable. The last loop copies the leftover 900.

questions.q: The payouts are sorted by amount (kobo). Print the two amounts that add up to the refund, as an array, or null. Use two pointers, not nested loops.
questions.explain: Too big: drop the right end; too small: drop the left end. At most n − 1 steps, O(1) extra space.

questions.q: Remove duplicate order ids from the sorted array in place with a reader and a writer. Print the number of unique ids and the array after truncating it.
questions.explain: The reader visits every element once; the writer advances only for a new id. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

questions.q: Find the middle stop of the linked route with fast and slow pointers (for an even number of stops, the second middle). Print its name.
questions.explain: The route is Lekki, Ajah, Ikoyi, Yaba, Ikeja. When fast has taken two double steps (to Ikoyi, then Ikeja, whose next is null), slow has taken two single steps, to Ikoyi.

questions.q: Each account forwards to at most one other (a Map). Using Floyd's fast and slow pointers, print whether following the forwards from the given account loops forever.
questions.explain: From dayo the walk reaches eze, who forwards to nobody, so the fast pointer runs out. From ada both pointers circle and meet. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: Merge the two sorted lists of amounts into one sorted list in O(n + m), without calling sort. Print the result joined with spaces.
questions.explain: One pointer per list; take the smaller head and advance only that pointer; then copy whatever remains. Each element is copied once.

questions.q: Print the largest amount of water any two panels can hold (width times the shorter height) using two pointers from the ends.
questions.explain: The two end panels (height 4, width 4) hold 16, and no narrower tank can be taller than 4. Always move the shorter side; on a tie either side is safe.

questions.q: A username is "mirror-safe" if it reads the same forwards and backwards once lower-cased, ignoring anything that is not a letter or digit. Check it with two pointers moving inwards (skip ignored characters as you go). Print both results.
questions.explain: Each branch moves at least one pointer, so the loop always ends. Skipping in place avoids building a cleaned copy: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

questions.q: An array of order totals uses 0 for cancelled orders. Move every non-zero total to the front in place, keeping their order, and fill the rest with zeros. Use a reader and a writer. Print the array.
questions.explain: The same reader/writer shape as in-place dedupe: the writer marks the next free slot for a kept value. The data need not be sorted here, because the keep rule (non-zero) does not compare neighbours. O(n) time, O(1) space.
